A is the starting-point of the world of sound:
even so is the Ancient one Supreme the starting-point of all that exists.
Of what avail is all thy learning if thou worship not the holy feet of Him of the perfect intelligence?
Behold the man who taketh refuge in the sacred feet of Him who walked on flowers:
his days will be many upon the earth.
Behold the men who cleave unto the feet of Him who is beyond preference and beyond aversion:
the ills of life touch them not ever.
Behold the men who sing earnestly the praise of the Lord;
they will be freed from the pain-engendering fruits of action both good and evil.
Behold the men who follow the righteous ways of Him who burned away the desires of the five senses;
their days will be many upon the earth.
They alone escape from sorrow who take refuge in the feet of Him who hath no equal.
The stormy seas of wealth and sense delights cannot be traversed except by those who cling to the feet of the Sage who is the Ocean of Righteousness.
Worthless indeed like the organs of sense which do not perceive is the head that boweth not at the feet of Him who is endowed with the eight attributes.
They alone cross the ocean of births and deaths who take refuge in the feet of the Lord;
the others traverse it not.
It is the unfailing fall of rain that sustaineth the earth:
look thou therefore upon it as very amrita - the drink immortal of the gods.
Every food that is sweet to the taste is the gift of rain to man:
and itself also formeth part of his food besides.
If rain should fail, famine would rage over the wide earth even though it is encircled by the ocean.
Husbandmen would cease to ply the plough if the fountains of the heavens are dried up.
It is rain that ruineth, and it is rain again that setteth up those that it hath ruined.
Even grass will cease to grow if the showers from above should cease to fall.
Even the mighty ocean would reek with corruption if the heavens should cease to suck its waters and render them back to it.
Sacrifice will not be offered to the Gods, nor feasts be celebrated on earth, if the heavens should be dried up.
Neither Charity nor Tapas will abide on the wide earth if the heavens should hold back their showers.
Nothing on earth can go without water;
that being so, the conduct of even most virtuously minded of men dependeth ultimately on rain.
Behold the men who have renounced sense-enjoyments and live a life of discipline;
the scriptures exalt their glory above every other good.
Thou canst not measure the greatness of the men of renunciation:
thou canst as well count the number of the dead.
Behold the men who have weighed this life with the next and have renounced the world:
the earth is made radiant by their greatness.
Behold the man whose firm will controlleth his five senses even as the goading hook controlleth the elephant:
he is a seed fit for the fields of heaven.
Dost thou desire to know the power of the saint who hath quenched the cravings of his five senses? Look on the king of the Gods, Indra:
his one example is enough.
The great ones are they who can achieve the impossible:
the feeble ones are those who cannot.
Behold the man who appreciateth at their true value the sensations of touch and taste and sight and sound and smell:
he will command the world.
The scriptures proclaim the greatness of the men of the mighty word.
It is impossible to support even for a moment the wrath of those who stand on the rock of renunciation.
Brahmans are also to be looked upon as men of renunciation:
for they have compassion on all life.
Righteousness leadeth unto heaven and it bringeth wealth also:
then what is there that is more profitable than righteousness?
There is no greater good than righteousness, nor no greater ill than the forgetting of it.
Be thou unremitting in the doing of good deeds:
do them with all thy might and by every means.
Be pure in heart: all righteousness is contained in this one commandment;
all other things are naught but empty display.
Avoid envy and greed, anger and harsh words;
that is the way to acquire righteousness.
Say not in thy heart, I shall be righteous by and by, but begin to do good works without delaying;
for it is righteousness will be thy undying companion on the day of thy death.
Ask me not, What will it profit a man if he is righteous? Look at the bearer of the palanquin and him that rideth on it.
If thou do good all thy life without a single wasted day, thou wallest up the road that leadeth unto future births.
They alone are joys which flow from a virtuous life:
All other pleasures end but in disgrace and sorrow.
That action alone is worth doing which is based on righteousness;
and all action must be shunned which will subject thee to the reproof of the wise.
The householder is the mainstay of all who follow the three other paths of life.
The houesholder is the friend of the pitris and the destitute, and of those who have renounced the world.

Five are the duties of the householder, namely, the offering of oblations to the pitris, the performance of sacrifice to the gods, the doing of hospitality, the rendering of help unto relations, and the looking after of one’s own self.
Behold the man who feareth the reproof of the wise and doth charity before eating his meal: his seed decayeth never.
If love aboundeth in the home and righteousness doth prevail, the home is perfect and its end is all fulfilled.
If a man fulfilled aright duties of the householder, where is the need for him to take up other duties?
Among those that seek after salvation, the greatest are they who lead a virtuous family life, performing aright all the duties that belong to it.
Behold the householder who helpeth others in the observance of their vows and who leadeth a virtuous life himself;
he is a greater saint than those who betake themselves to a life of fasting and prayer.
Righteousness belongeth especially to the married life;
and a good name is its ornament.
The householder who liveth as he ought to live will be looked upon as a god among men.
She is the good helpmate who possesseth every wifely virtue and spendeth not above her husband’s means.
All other blessings turn to nought if the wife faileth in wifely virtues.
Where is indigence if the wife is worthy, and where is wealth if worth is not in her?
What is there that is grander than woman, when she is strong in the strength of her chastity?
Behold the woman who worshippeth not the Gods, but worshippeth her husband even as she riseth from bed:
the rain cloud obeyeth her commands.
She is the good household who guardeth her virtue and her reputation, and tendeth her husband with loving care.
Of what avail is close confinement? It is her own continence that is the best guardian of a womans virtue.
Behold the woman who hath begotten a (worthy) son:
her place is high in the world of the gods.
Behold the man whose home beareth not an honourable reputation;
the proud, lion-like walk in the sight of detractors is denied to him.
The chiefest blessing is an honourable home;
and its crowning glory is worthy offspring.
We know of no blessing so great as the begetting of children that have knowledge surely won.
Behold the man whose children bear an unstained character:
no evil will touch him up to his seventh reincarnation.
Children are the veritable riches of a man;
for they pass to him by their acts all the merits that they acquire.
Sweeter verily than ambrosia is the gruel soused and spattered by the tender hands of ones own children.
The touch of children is the delight of the body;
the delight of the ear is the hearing of their speech.
The flute is sweet and the guitar dulcet;
so say they who have not heard the babbling speech of their little ones.
munti iruppac ceyal. What is the duty of the father to his son? It is to make him worthy to sit in the front rank in the assembly.
It is a joy of every man to find himself eclipsed in intelligence by his children.
Great is the joy of the mother when a man child is born unto her:
but greater far is her delight when she heareth him called worthy.
What is the duty of the son to his father? It is to make the world ask, For what austerities of his hath he been blessed with such a son?
Where is the bar that can close in the gate of love? The gentle tear-drops that form themselves in the eye of lovers are sure to proclaim its presence.
Those that love not live only for themselves;
as to those that love, they will give their very bones for helping others.
They say it is to taste again of love that soul hath consented once more to be encased in bone.
Love maketh the heart tender towards all;
and tenderness yieldeth that price less treasure called friendship.
The blessing of the blessed, they say, is nothing but a reward of the gods for a nature that had been full of loving-tenderness in the past.
They are fools who say that love is for the righteous alone:
for even against the evil-minded love is the only ally for a man.
Behold how the sun burneth the boneless worm;
even so doth Righteousness burn the man that doth not love.
Behold the man whose heart knoweth not what love is:
he will know prosperity only when the sapless tree of the desert putteth forth leaves.
Of what avail is a lovely outside, if love the souls ornament, hath no place in the heart?
The seat of life is in Love;
the man who hath it not is only a mass of skin-encased bone.
What for do the wise toil and set up homes? It is to feed the guest and help the pilgrim.
Were it even the draught of immortality it shall not be tasted alone when the guest is in the hall.
No evil can befall the man who never faileth to honour the incoming guest.
Behold the man who receiveth the worthy guest with his best smile:
Lakshmi delighteth to abide in his home.
Behold the man who feedeth his guest first and then only eateth what is left;
doth his land stand in need even of sowing?
Behold the man who hath tended the out-going guest and waiteth for the incoming one;
he is a welcome guest unto the gods.
We cannot say of any hospitable act by itself, so much is the merit of this act:
it is the worth of the guest that is the measure of the sacrifice.
Behold the man who performeth not the sacrifice of hospitality:
he will say one day. I have toiled hard and laid me up a great treasure: but is all in vain, for there is none to comfort me.
Not to honour the pilgrim is veritable indigence in the midst of wealth:
such a thing is to be found only with fools.
The anitcha flower fadeth when thou holdest it near the nose and smellest it:
but a mere look is enough to break the heart of the great.
The speech that is truly kind is the speech of the righteous man which is full of tenderness and free from dissimulation.
Better than a generous gift is sweet speech and a kind gracious look.
Behold the sweet and gracious look and the kind speech that cometh from the heart;
Righteousness hath is dwelling place there.
Behold the man who always speaketh sweet words whosoever it be to whom he speaketh:
Poverty, the increaser of sorrow, will never come near him.
Modesty and loving speech, these alone are ornaments to a man, and none other.
Sinfulness will wane away and righteousness will increase if thy thoughts are good and thy speech is kind.
The word that is serviceable and kind createth friends and bringeth forth benefits.
Words that are kind and are removed from all littleness yield good in this life and in the next also.
How doth a man continue to use violent words, even after he hath felt the pleasure that kind words give?
Behold the man who useth hard words when sweet ones serve;
he preferreth the unripe fruit to the ripe.
Behold the kindness done without any obligation;
even the heavens and the earth but poorly paid.
A kindness done in the hour of need may look small;
but it outweigheth the whole world.
Behold the kindness done without thought of recompense:
the ocean will look small when compared with its worth.
The benefit received may be small even like a tiny millet seed:
but in the eyes of the worthy its measure is that of a mighty palmyra tree.
Gratitude is not to be measured merely by the measure of the assistance given;
its measure is alone the nobility of him that receiveth the benefit.
Forget not the friendship of the holy ones:
nor forsake those that succoured thee in thy difficulty.
The worthy will remember with gratitude even unto their seventh reincarnation those that succoured them in their need.
It is ignoble to forget a kindness;
but an injury received, it is the part of nobility to forget at once.
The mortallest injury is forgiven the moment the mind recalleth a single kindness received from the injurer.
There is redemption for men who are guilty of every other crime;
but the ungrateful wretch shall know of none.
The Alpha and Omega of righteous life is propriety;
and propriety requireth that thou must give each man his due whether he be a stranger, or a friend, or an enemy.
The prosperity of the joy groweth not less:
it endureth even unto their remotest posterity.
Though nought but profit come of it, touch not the wealth that cometh by deviating from the right.
The worthy and the unworthy are known by their offspring.
Evil and good come unto all;
but his upright heart is the glory of the man of worth.
When thy heart swerveth from the right and turneth unto evil, know that thy destruction is near at hand.
The world looketh not down on the poverty of the upright and virtuous man.
Behold the weighing beam, for it is straight in itself and weigheth justly:
the glory of the wise is to be like unto it and to incline neither to this side nor to that.
Verily the upright speech coming out of mans mouth is a judgement, provided that he swerveth not at all from the right in his heart.
Behold the business man that looketh after the interests of others as his own; his business will expand.
Self-control leadeth unto heaven, but uncontrolled passion is the royal road to endless darkness.
Guard thy self-control as a very treasure;
life hath no richer wealth here below.
Behold the man who rateth the thing of this world at their true value and liveth a life of self-control;
wisdom and every other blessing will come unto him.
Behold the man who hath triumphed over his passions and who swerveth not from duty:
his form is more imposing than a mountain.
Humility is beautiful in all men;
but alone on the rich doth it shine in all its splendour.
Behold the man who can draw in into himself his five senses even as the tortoise doth its limbs:
he hath laid up for himself a treasure that will last even unto his seventh reincarnation.
Whatever else thou rein not in, rein in thy tongue;
for an unbridled tongue will utter foolish things and will lead thee unto grief.
If even one word of thine causeth pain to another, all thy virtue is lost.
The burn caused by fire healeth in its time:
but the wound burned in by the tongue remaineth a running sore for ever.
Behold the man who hath learned wisdom and self-control and who alloweth not anger to harbour in his heart:
Righteousness pilgrimageth to his home in order to have a sight of his face.
The man whose conduct is pure is honoured by all:
purity of conduct is therefore to be prized even above life.
Watch anxiously over thy conduct;
for wheresover thou mayest search thou canst not find a firmer ally than right conduct.
A pure life bespeaketh an honourable family:
but low conduct placeth a man amongst the ignoble.
Even the Vedas if forgotten can be learned again:
but once fallen from virtuous conduct the Brahman is fallen from his place for ever.
Prosperity is not for the envious:
even so dignity is not for men of impure conduct.
The firm-minded swerve not from virtuous conduct;
for they know the evils brought on by such swerving.
The man of right conduct is honoured among men:
but ignominy alone is the portion of those who fall therefrom.
Purity of conduct soweth the seed of prosperity:
but an evil course is the mother of endless ills.
Foul words can never fall from the lips of the well-bred even when off their guard.
Fools may be as instructed as thou pleasest;
but they never learn to conform to the ways of the Righteous.
Behold the men whose eyes are turned towards righteousness and towards wealth:
they commit not the folly of desiring another mans wife.
Among those that have fallen from virtue there is no greater fool than he that haunteth the household of another.
Verily they are in the jaws of death who invade the home of an unsuspecting friend.
Let a man be ever so great:
what availeth it all if he committeth adultery without thinking ever so little of the shame that floweth therefrom?
Behold the man who hangeth on to his neighbours wife because she is accessible;
his name is sullied for ever.
The adulterer knoweth no respite from four things, hatred, sin, fear and shame.
He is the righteous householder whose heart is not attracted by the charms of his neighbours wife.
Behold the high-souled man that looketh not on anothers wife:
he is more than righteous; he is saintly.
Who on earth deserve all the good things of the world? It is they who clasp not the arms of her who belongeth to another.
Though thou shouldst transgress and yield to every other sin, abstain at least from the sin of adultery;
that abstention will bring thee credit.
The earth supporteth even those that dig into her entrails:
even so bear thou with those that traduce thee: for that is greatness.
Forgive thou always the injuries that others may do thee;
but if thou forget them it were even better.
The most shameful poverty is the refusal of hospitality:
and the greatest strength is to bear with the dullness of fools.
If thou wantest to be grand always, cultivate with patience the habit of forgiving others transgression.
The wise think not much of the men who retaliate an injury:
but they are prized as gold who forgive their enemy.
The joy of revenge lasteth but a day;
but the glory of him who forgiveth endureth for ever.
Let the wrong suffered be ever so great;
the better part is not to take it to heart and to abstain from revenge.
Conquer by thy nobility those that in their pride have injured thee.
More saintly than even those that have renounced are they that bear with the bitter tongue of their detractors.
Those that do penance by fasting are great;
but they only come after those that forgive their calumniators.
Know that thy heart is inclining towards virtue when thou findest that it is free from all feelings of envy.
No blessing is so great as a nature that is free from all envy.
It is he that careth not for virtue or for wealth that envieth his neighbours prosperity instead of rejoicing at it.
The wise injure not others through envy;
for they know the evils that result from entertaining that mean feeling.
Envy itself is scourge enough for the envious men;
for, even if his enemies spare him, his own envy will work his ruin.
Behold the man that beareth not to see gifts made to another;
his family will beg for very food and clothing and perish.
Lakshmi cannot bear with the envious she will quit their side, leaving them to the care of her elder sister.
Caitiff Envy bringeth on indigence and leadeth up to the gates of hell.
The affluence of the envious and the misery of the generous-minded are alike matter for wonder.
Never hath envy led to prosperity;
nor a generous heart to a fall therefrom.
Behold the unscrupulous man who coveteth another mans wealth:
his wickednesses will increase and his family will decline.
Behold the men that turn away from evil:
they covet not, neither do they yield to ignoble deeds.
Behold the men that care for other joys;
they are not greedy after little delights, nor do they yield unto iniquity.
Behold the men that have mastered their senses and enlarged their vision:
they covet not saying, Lo, we are in want.
Of what avail is a mind that is subtle and comprehending, if it yieldeth unto greed and consenteth unto insensate deeds?
Even he who hungereth after grace and walketh in the path will perish if he hankereth after wealth and plotteth evil.
Covet not the wealth that greed gathereth;
for its fruit is bitter in the day of enjoyment.
If thou desire that thy substance should not grow less, covet not the riches in thy neighbours hands.
Behold the wise man that understandeth justice and coveteth not;
Lakshmi knoweth his worth and seeketh him in his home.
The greed that looketh not beyond engendereth destruction;
but the greatness that sayeth, I desire, not triumpheth over all.
Behold the man who doth iniquity and who would not so much as even utter the name of righteousness;
it is sweet even unto him if men say, Lo, here is one who backbiteth not.
It is wrong to turn away from good and do evil:
but it is far worse to smile before and vilify behind.
It is worthier to die at once than live by lying and slander:
for such a death bringeth with it the fruits of righteousness.
Slander not a man behind his back even though he hath insulted thee to thy very face.
The lips may speak righteousness;
but a slanderous tongue betrayeth the meanness of the heart.
If thou slander another, he will look into thy own transgressions and expose the worst of them.
Behold the men who delight in slander:
they know not the sweet art of making friends, and will drive away from themselves even their old friends disgusted.
Those that love to speak abroad the transgressions of their friends, how will they spare the transgressions of their enemies?
May it be that the Earth calleth her sense of duty to her aid in supporting the weight of the backbiting slanderer?
If a man can scan his own faults as he doth those of his enemies, can evil ever come to him?
Behold the man that angereth his hearers by the speaking of vain words:
he will be despised of all men.
Worse even than injuring ones friends is the speaking of vain words before many.
He that multiplieth empty words declareth loud his want of worth.
Behold the man that speaketh vain words in an assembly;
no profit will come unto him and all that is good will flee from his side.
Even the worthy will lose honour and respect if they indulge in vain speaking.
Call not him man who loveth idle words;
call him rather a chaff among men.
Let the wise, if they deem it meet, speak even hard words;
but it is good for them to desisit from profitless speech.
The wise whose thoughts are set on the solution of great problems utter no words that are not full of deep significance.
They whose eyes are whole say not vain words even by oversight.
Speak thou only such words as are worth saying;
and speak not ever words that are profitless and vain.
The evil fear not the folly called sin;
but the worthy flee from it.
Evil bringeth forth evil; evil therefore is to be feared even more than fire.
The chiefest wisdom, they say, is to abstain from injury even to an enemy.
Let not a man compass anothers ruin even unthinkingly;
for Justice will compass the ruin of him that plotteth evil.
Let not a man work evil saying, I am poor:
for if he do, he will sink into a lower destitution than before.
Whose desireth not to be saddened by ill, let him abstain from doing injury to others.
There is a way of escape from every other enemy:
but ill deeds never die but pursue and destroy their author.
As the shadow leaveth not a man but doggeth his footsteps wheresoever he goeth, even so do evil deeds pursue their author and work his destruction.
If a man love his own self, let him not incline his mind towards evil in any degree.
Know that man to be secure from ills who leaveth not the straight path in order to commit wrong.
The gracious expect no return when they oblige:
how can the world ever repay the rain-cloud?
The substance gathered in by the worthy by the labour of their hands is all for others use.
A better thing than a gracious complaisance cannot be had either here or in heaven.
He alone liveth who knoweth what is proper:
he who knoweth not what is fitting shall be classed with the dead.
Behold the village tank filled with water to its brim;
like unto it is the prosperity of the wise man that loveth the world.
Like unto a fruit-tree in the middle of the village bearing fruit is riches in the hands of the man of heart.
Like unto a tree that yieldeth medicinal drugs and is available to all is riches in the hands of the obliging man.
Behold the men who know what is just and proper;
they fail not to oblige others even when fallen on evil days.
The complaisant man thinketh himself poor only when he is impotent to oblige those who solicit his aid.
If ruin cometh as a result of complaisance it is worth courting even by selling ones own self into slavery.
Giving to the poor is alone charity:
all other giving is of the nature of loan.
Though it lead unto heaven, receiving is bad, and though heaven should be denied to the giver, even then the giving of alms would be the highest virtue.
It is only the highborn man that giveth without ever meanly saying I have not.
The heart of the giver is not glad until he seeth the smile of content on the face of the suppliant.
The conquest of conquests to the conqueror over self is the conquest over hunger;
but even that conquest cometh only after the self-abnegation of him who appeaseth that hunger.
To fill the gnawing hunger of the poor;
that is the way that the wealthy man should lay up a store for himself against an evil day.
The evil disease called hunger toucheth not the man that divideth his bread with others.
The hard of heart who perish their wealth by hoarding it, have not they ever tasted the delight of giving unto others?
Bitterer verily than the beggars bread is the hoarded meal of the miser eating alone.
Nothing is bitterer than death;
but even death is sweet when one hath not the wherewithal to give to those who appeal for help.
Give to the poor and add glory unto thy name:
there is no greater profit for man than this.
The one theme in the mouth of all that praise is the glory of those that give unto the poor.
Everything else dieth on earth:
but the fame of those grand men whose achievements are unique in the annals of mankind endureth for ever.
Behold the man that hath won a lasting, world-wide fame:
the Gods on high prefer him even before saints.
The ruin that addeth unto fame and the death that bringeth glory are impossible of attainment except only by men of soul.
Having come into this world, let a man acquire glory and fame:
as to those who have not achieved fame, it is better for them not to have been born at all.
Those that are not free from blemish chafe not at themselves:
why then are they wroth against their calumniators?
It is a disgrace for all men if they earn not the memory called fame.
Behold the land weighed down beneath the tread of an inglorious people;
though famed for its wealth in the past, it will be reduced to utter poverty.
They alone live who live without blemish;
and they alone die who have lived without glory.
The chiefest wealth is a heart that over floweth with mercy;
for material wealth is found even in the hands of vile men.
Follow the good path and learn to be merciful:
and if thou examine the teachings of other faiths also, thou wilt see that Mercy is the only Salvation.
They enter not into the dark and bitter world whose heart is joined unto mercy.
The results of actions at which the soul trembleth pursue not him who is kind and merciful to all life.
Vexation never toucheth the merciful:
the teeming air-encircled earth is a witness thereto.
Behold the man that hath forsaken mercy and doth inequity:
though he must have suffered cruelly in past births for neglecting mercy, he hath forgotten the lesson, say the wise.
The other world is not for those whose heart is incapable of pity, even as this world is not for them that are without riches.
The poor in substance may one day thrive and prosper:
but they that lack pity are poor indeed and their day cometh never.
It is as easy for the hard of heart to do deeds of righteousness as for the confused in mind to see the Truth.
When thou art tempted to oppress the weak, call to mind how thou feltest within thyself when thou didst tremble before a stronger.
How can he feel pity, who eateth other flesh in order to fatten his own?
Thou canst not find riches in the hands of the thriftless:
even so thou canst not find pity in the hearts of those that eat meat.
The heart of the man that tasteth flesh turneth not towards good, even as the heart of him that is armed with steel.
The killing of animals is veritable hardness of heart;
but the eating of their flesh is inequity indeed.
In non-eating of flesh is Life:
if thou eat, the pit of hell will not open its mouth to let thee out.
If the world desireth not meat for eating there will be none to offer it for sale?
If a man can only realize to himself the agony and pain suffered by other living beings, he would not desire to eat fleshmeat.
Behold the men who have escaped from the bonds of illusion and ignorance:
they eat not the flesh from which life hath flown out.
To abstain from the killing and eating of living beings is better than to perform a thousand sacrifices in the sacrificial fire.
Behold the man who killeth not and abstaineth from flesh meat:
all the world joineth hands to do him reverence.
Patient endurance of suffering and non- injuring of life, in these is contained the whole of tapas.
Tapas is possible only for those who have acquired merit by tapas in previous births;
it is profitless for others to take it up.
Is it because there should be some people to tend and feed ascetics that all the rest have neglected tapas?
If thou wouldst destroy thy foes and exalt those that love thee, know that such a power belongeth unto tapas.
Tapas fulfilleth all desires even in the very manner that is desired;
therefore is it that men endeavour after tapas in this world.
It is the men that do tapas that look after their own interests:
the rest are caught in the snares of desire and only do themselves harm.
The fiercer the fire in which it is melted, the more brilliant becometh the lusture of the gold:
even so, the severer the sufferings endured by the austere in the performance of their tapas, the purer their nature shineth.
Behold the man who hath attained mastery over himself:
all other men worship him.
Behold the men that have acquired power by austerities:
they can succeed even in conquering death.
If the needy are the many in the world, it is because those that do tapas are few, and those that do not, form the larger number.
The five principles of his own body smile within themselves when they see the imposture of the hypocrite.
Of what avail is an imposing presence when evil is in the heart and the heart is conscious thereof?
Behold the man who hath not attained mastery over himself putting on the puissant look of the austere:
he is like a cow that grazeth about wearing a tigers skin.
Behold the man who taketh cover under a saintly garb and doth evil:
he is like a fowler hiding in the bush and decoying birds.
The hypocrite pretendeth unto sanctity and sayeth, I have vanquished my passion:
but he will come to grief and cry, what have I done! oh, what have I done!.
Behold the man that hath not renounced in his heart, but walketh about like one that hath renounced, and cheateth men:
thou canst not find a more unscrupulous villain than him.
The kunri seed is fair on one side, but the other side of it is black:
there are men who are like unto it: they are fair on the outside, but their inside is all foul.
Many there be whose heart is impure but who bathe in holy streams and prowl about.
The arrow is straight but thirsts for blood, while the lute that hath a bend radiates harmony around:
judge thou therefore men by their acts and not by their appearance.
Neither matted hair thou wantest nor shaven head, if thou abstain from that which the world condemneth.
Who so wanteth not to be held in contempt, let him guard himself against every thought of fraud.
It is a sin even to say in ones heart, I shall cheat my neighbour of his substance.
The fortune that is built up by fraud may appear to thrive:
but it is doomed for ever.
The thirst for plunder leadeth in its season to endless grief.
Behold the man that coveteth other mens substance and lieth in wait to catch them napping:
he thinketh not of grace and love is far from his heart.
The man who thirsteth after plunder cannot weigh things aright:
nor can he walk in the way of righteousness.
Behold the man that hath weighed the things of this world and made his heart firm:
he committeth not the folly of cheating his neighbour.
As righteousness resideth in the heart of him who valueth things aright, even so Deceit hath its seat in the heart of the thief.
Behold the man who meditateth on nothing but fraud and deceit:
he will leave the right path and perish.
He that deceiveth others is not master even of his own body:
but the world of the Gods itself is a never failing inheritance unto those that are upright.
What is truthfulness? It is the speaking of that which is free from even the slightest taint of evil.
Even falsehood is of the nature of truth if it bringeth forth unmixed good.
Hold not forth as truth what thou knowest to be false;
for thy own conscience will burn thee when thou hast lied.
Behold the man whose heart is free from every trace of falsehoold:
he reigneth in the hearts of all.
Behold the man whose heart is fixed in truthfulness:
he is greater than the austere and greater than he that maketh gifts to the poor.
There is no greater renown for a man than the renown that he is a stranger unto falsehood:
such a man acquireth every virtue without mortifying the body.
If a man can live without ever uttering a falsehood, all other virtues are superfluous unto him.
Water cleanseth but the outward form;
but the purity of the heart is proved by truthfulness.
The worthy regard not all other light as light;
it is only the light of truth that they look upon as a veritable illumination.
Many things have I seen in this world;
but of all the things that I have seen, there is nothing that is higher than truth.
A man can be said to forbear only when he hath the power to strike and striketh not:
Where he hath not the power, what mattereth it whether he forbeareth or beareth not?
It is wrong to get angry even when thou art helpless to strike;
and when thou hast the power, there is nothing that is worse than anger.
Whoever thy offender may be, forget thy anger;
for from anger spring a multitude of ills.
Anger killeth the smile and it destroyeth cheer:
hath man a crueller foe than anger?
If thou want to look after thyself, keep off from choler;
for if thou keep not off, it will come upon thee and destroy thy own self.
Choler destroyeth every man whom it approacheth:
and it burneth also the family of him who nurseth it.
He who nurseth his rage as if it were a precious thing is like unto the man who dasheth his hand against the ground:
the hand of this man escapeth not from injury, and the destruction of the first is as certain.
Even when thy wrongs burn as the flaming of many fires, it is good if thou canst abstain from anger.
All the desires of a man will be fulfilled on the instant if from his heart he banish anger.
Whoso is overwhelmed with anger is like one dead;
but whoso hath forsworn wrath-fulness is like unto the saints.
The man who is pure in heart would not injure others even if he could obtain a princely estate thereby.
Even when another hath injured him in his hate, the man who is pure in heart returneth not the injury.
If thou injure another, even though it be only a man who hath injured thee without any provocation, thou simply bringest down upon thyself evils that can never be remedied.
How shall a man punish them that have injured him? Let him do them a good turn and make them ashamed in their hearts.
Of what avail is intelligence to a man if he doth not feel as his very own the pain suffered by other beings and so feeling doth not abstain from injuring any?
When a man hath felt a pain for himself, let him take care that he inflicteth it not on others.
It is a great thing, if thou injure not knowingly any man, at any time, and in any degree.
He who hath felt what pain meaneth to himself, how doth he bring himself to inflict it on others?
If a man injureth his neighbour in the forenoon evil will come to him in the afternoon of its own accord.
All evil recoileth on the head of the wrong doer;
they abstain therefore from wrong-doing who desire to be immune from ills.
The greatest of virtues is non-killing:
killing bringeth in its train every other sin.
To divide one’s bread with the needy and abstain from killing;
these are the greatest of all the commandments of all the prophets.
The greatest virtue of all is non-killing:
truthfulness cometh only next.
What is the good way? It is the path that taketh thought how it may save even the smallest of creatures from being killed.
Among all those that have renounced family life with its fears of ill, the chiefest is he that reverenceth all life for fear of killing any.
Behold the man who hath taken the vow of non-killing:
Death that eateth away all life maketh no inroads into his days.
Take not away from any living thing the life that is sweet unto all, even if it be to save thine own.
They may say, Sacrifices gain for a man many blessings:
but to the pure in heart the blessings that are earned by killing are an abomination.
Those who live by slaying are likened by the discriminating to eaters of carrion.
Behold the beggar whose putrid body is festering with ulcerous sores;
he must have been a shedder of blood in the past, say the wise.
There is no greater folly than the infatuation that looketh upon the transient as if it were everlasting.
The crowd that assembleth to witness a village show, that is the symbol of great riches flowing on a man:
and the dispersal of the same crowd is the type of its passing away.
Prosperity is transient: if thou have come by it, delay not to do things that are of lasting good.
Time looketh like an innocent thing:
but verily it is a saw that is continually sawing away the life of man.
Make haste to do good works before the tongue is paralysed and hiccough ariseth in the throat.
But yesterday a man was and today he is not:
that is the wonder of wonders in this world.
Man knoweth not if he shall last the next minute:
but his thoughts are more than ten million.
The fledgeling abandoneth the broken shell of the egg and flieth away:
that is the symbol of the love between the soul and the body.
Death is like unto a sleep:
and life is like the waking after that sleep.
tuccil irunta uyirkku. Hath the soul no fixed home of its own, that it seeketh a lodging in this worthless body?
Whatsoever thing a man hath renounced, from the grief arising from that hath he liberated himself.
If thou want joy, renounce early:
for many are the delights that thou shalt enjoy after renouncing.
Crush thou the five senses:
and everything in which thou takest delight, give up utterly.
To possess nothing, that is the law of the man of vows:
the possession of even one thing is a coming back to the snares that he hath left.
To those that desire to put an end to their reincarnations, even the body is a superfluity:
how much more then are other bonds?
uyarnta ulakam pukum. The feelings of I and Mine are nought but vanity and pride;
he who crusheth them entereth a higher world than the world of the gods.
Behold the man who holdeth on to attachments and giveth not them up;
Care and Sorrow will take hold of him and will not give him up.
They that have renounced utterly are on the path to salvation;
but the others are caught in a snare.
The moment that attachments are broken, that very moment reincarnations cease:
the man who breaketh them not continueth in vanity.
Attach and tie thyself to Him who hath conquered all attachments;
bind thyself firmly to Him in order that all thy bonds may be broken.
Behold the delusion that taketh vanities for the Reality:
it bringeth the soul again into this world of sorrow.
Behold the man who hath freed himself from delusion and whose vision is unclouded and clear:
darkness ceaseth for him and joy cometh unto him.
Behold the man who hath freed himself from doubts and who hath realised the Truth:
heaven is nearer to him than earth.
Though risen to human birth, the soul hath profited nothing if it hath not realised the Truth.
To separate the true from the false in everything, whatever its nature may be, that is the part of a wise understanding.
Behold the man who hath studied deeply and hath realised the Truth;
he will enter the path that leadeth not again into this world.
Verily those that have meditated upon and attained to the Truth need not think at all of future incarnations.
He is the wise man who endeavoureth after perfection and Truth in order that he might escape the folly of being born again.
Behold the man who understandeth the means of his salvation and laboureth to conquer all attachments:
the ills that he is yet to suffer depart from him.
All suffering ceaseth for a man when he hath conquered utterly desire and anger and delusion.
Desire is the seed that yieldeth unto every soul, and always, a never failing crop of births.
If thou must needs long for anything, long for freedom from reincarnation and that freedom will come to thee if thou long to conquer longing.
There is no greater wealth here below than desirelessness and even in heaven thou canst find no treasure that equalleth it.
Purity is nought but freedom from desire:
and this freedom is achieved by yearning after perfect truthfulness.
It is those that have conquered their desire that are called the librated ones:
the others appear to be free but they are verily in bondage.
If thou love righteousness, flee from desire;
for desire is a snare and a disappointment.
If a man crusheth utterly all desire, salvation will come to him by any path that he commandeth to it.
He that hath no desires hath no grief;
but ills on ills descend on the man that hanke - reth after things.
Even here a man shall have everlasting joy if he killeth that greatest misery of all, desire.
Desire is never filled; but if a man giveth it up utterly he attaineth perfection even at the very moment of giving it up.
Resolution cometh to a man when Fortune is about to smile to him;
but Indolence appeareth when Fortune is about to leave.
Evil fate dulleth the faculties;
but when Fortune is about to smile on a man, she first expandeth his intelligence.
What doth learning avail and all subtleties? When Destiny driveth, it is the native blindness that prevaileth over all.
The world falleth into two categories that are mutually exclusive:
for success in life is one thing and saintliness quite another.
When the tide is against thee even good things turn to evil:
and even evil things turn to good when the tide is on.
What Destiny denieth thou canst not keep even with the utmost care;
and even if thou throw them away wilfully the things that are thine will not go away from thee.
Even the man who hath amassed ten million cannot enjoy his riches except as the Ordainer hath ordained.
Verily the destitute poor would turn their hearts towards renunciation but that Destiny reserveth them for the miseries that are their portion.
They that rejoice when good cometh, why should they fret when they encounter evil?
What is there that is mightier than destiny? For even as its victim is meditating a plan to overcome it, it forestalleth him and bringeth him down. The material world
He is a lion among princes who is well endowed in respect of the six things, to wit, troops, population, substance, council, alliances, and fortifications.
Four qualities should never be wanting in the prince, namely, courage, liberality, sagacity and energy.
Behold the men that are destined to rule the earth:
the three virtues, alertness, learning and quickness of decision, leave them not.
The prince shall not fail in virtue and shall abolish unrighteousness:
he shall guard his honour jealously but shall not sin against the laws of valour.
vakuttalum vallatu aracu. The prince shall know how to develop the resources of his kingdom and how to enrich his treasury:
how to preserve his wealth and how to spend it worthily.
If the prince is accessible to all his subjects and is never harsh of word, his kingdom will be esteemed above every other.
Behold the prince who can give with grace and rule with love;
his fame will fill the earth, and whatever land he desireth to conquer will be sure to come under his sway.
Behold the prince who administreth impartial justice and protecteth his subjects:
he will be looked upon as a god among men.
Behold the prince who hath the virtue to bear with words that are bitter to the ear;
his subjects will never leave the shadow of his umbrella.
Behold the prince who is liberal and gracious and just, and who tendeth his people with care;
he is a light among kings.
Acquire thoroughly the knowledge that is worth acquiring:
and after acquiring it walk thou in accordance therewith.
Two are the eyes of living kind:
the one is called Numbers, and the other, Letters.
The learned alone can be said to possess eyes:
the unlettered have but two sores in their head.
It is a festival of joy when learned men come together:
but wistful grow their hearts when the time of their parting arriveth.
Though thou hast to humble thyself before the teacher even as a beggar before a man of wealth, thou yet acquirest learning:
it is those that refuse to learn that are the lowest among men.
Knowledge is like unto a sand spring;
the more thou diggest and drawest thereat, the more excellent is the flow thereof.
Everywhere is his home to the learned man, and everywhere his native land:
why then doth a man neglect instruction upto his dying day?
The learning that a man acquireth in this birth will exalt him even unto his seventh reincarnation.
The learned man seeth that the learning that delighteth him delighteth also all that listen to him;
and he loveth instruction all the more on that account.
An imperishable and flawless treasure is learning to a man;
other wealth is as nothing before it.
Ascending the rostrum without abundant knowledge is like the playing of dice without the chequered board.
Behold the man without instruction who desireth to be called eloquent;
he is like unto a woman without busts who yearneth to be admired of men.
Even a fool will be counted wise if he could hold his peace before the learned.
The man without instruction may be as wise as thou pleasest:
but the wise will attach no value to his opinions.
Behold the man who hath neglected instruction but who is wise in his own eyes;
he will be put to shame directly if he openeth his lips in an assembly.
Like unto a wasteland that yieldeth no harvests is the man that has neglected instruction:
all that men can say about him is that he liveth, and nothing more.
Behold the man whose understanding hath not been penetrated by the grand and the subtle;
the comeliness of his person is no better than the beauty of an image of clay.
Bitter verily is the poverty of the man of learning:
but far worse is riches in the hands of the fool.
The fool though born of a higher family is esteemed much less than a learned man who is of inferior descent.
How much better are men than beasts? Even so much are the learned better than those that have not cared for instruction.
The most precious of treasures is the treasure of the ear:
Verily it is the crown of all kinds of wealth.
Even unto the stomach some food will be offered when there is no food for the time being for the ear.
Behold the men who have listened to much instruction:
they are the very Gods on earth.
Let a man listen to instruction even though he hath no learning:
for it will be a stay unto him when he is encompassed by difficulty.
The counsel of the righteous is like unto a strong staff;
for it keepeth those that listen to it from slipping.
Listen to good words though they be but few;
even those few will add to thee a proportionate dignity.
Behold the man that hath mediated much in himself and hath laid by a store of instruction by listening to the discourses of the wise;
he talketh not nonsense even when in error.
Deaf indeed, though it heareth, is the ear that hath not been drilled by words of instruction.
Humility of speech is hard to be attained by those who have not listened to the subtle words of the wise.
Behold the men that taste with the tongue but know not the taste of the ear:
what doth it matter to the world whether they live or die?
The understanding is an armour against all surprise:
it is a fortress which even enemies cannot storm.
The disciplined understanding curbeth the senses from roving about, keepeth them from evil, and directeth them towards the Good.
To separate the true from the false in every utterance, whoever it be that speaketh, that is the part of a wise understanding.
What he speaketh, the wise man speaketh so as to be understood by all:
and from the lips of others he gathereth their subtle meanings.
The wise man attacheth all men to himself;
and his temper is ever even, neither expanding nor contracting to excess.
It is a part of wisdom to conform to the ways of the world.
The man of understanding knoweth what is coming;
but the fool foreseeth not what is before.
It is folly to rush headlong into danger:
It is the part of the wise to fear what ought to be feared.
Behold the man of foresight who is armed for every contingency;
he will never know the blow that causeth trembling.
He that hath understanding hath everything;
but the fool though he possesses everything hath nothing.
Behold the man who is free from haughtiness and anger and littleness:
there is a dignity about him that adorneth his prosperity.
Parsimony, over confidence and excessive amour Propre are faults in the prince.
Behold the men who are jealous of their reputation:
though their fault be small even like a millet seed; they look upon it as of the measure of a palmyra palm.
Guard thyself jealously against weaknesses:
for they are the foes that will lead thee to ruin.
Behold the man who provideth not before hand against surprise:
he will be destroyed even like a stack of straw before a spark of fire.
If the prince correcteth his own faults and looketh into those of others, where is the ill that can approach him?
Behold the miser that spendeth not where he ought to spend:
his wealth will come to an inglorious wreck.
Close-fisted parsimony is not a vice to be classed with other vices: it formeth a class apart.
Exult not at anything any time:
embark not on enterprises that would bring thee no good.
If thou canst keep from the knowledge of others the things in which thy heart taketh delight, the machinations of thy foes will be in vain.
Esteem thou the men that have grown old in righteousness, and acquire their friendship.
Behold the men who can cure the evils that have already befallen thee and who can guard thee from future ones:
cultivate thou their friendship with ardour.
It will be the rarest of rare good fortunes if thou canst secure to thyself the devotion of men of worth.
If those that are worthier than thyself have become thy intimates, thou hast acquired a strength before which all other strength paleth.
As the eyes of the prince are his own ministers, let him use his discretion and choose them wisely.
Behold the man who can move with the worthy as their intimate:
his foes will be powerless against him.
Who can ruin the man that commandeth the friendship of those that can reprove him?
Behold the prince who reposeth not on the support of men who can rebuke him;
he will perish even when he hath no foes.
Profit is not for those that have no capital:
even so stability is not for them that repose not on the firm support of the wise.
It is foolish to make a multitude of foes;
but it is ten times worse to give up the intimacy of the good.
Men of worth fear vulgar company;
but little minded men mix with it as if they made one family with it.
Water altereth and taketh the character of the soil through which it floweth;
even so the mind taketh the colour of the company with which it consorteth.
The understanding of a man belongeth unto his mind:
but his reputation dependeth on the company he keepeth.
The disposition of a man seemeth to reside in his mind:
but its veritable abode is the company in which he moveth.
Purity of heart and purity of action depend upon the purity of a mans company.
The pure of heart will have a righteous progeny:
and every thing prospereth unto those that consort with good company.
Purity of heart is a treasure unto a man:
and virtuous company bringeth him every glory.
Though themselves are endowed with every virtue, the wise look upon the company of the worthy as a tower of strength.
Virtue leadeth unto heaven;
and the company of the good steadieth a man in the practice thereof.
There is no greater ally to a man than good company;
and nothing bringeth greater troubles than evil company. Terintu ceyalvakai - Deliberation before Action
Take into consideration the output and the wastage and the profit that an undertaking will yield;
and then put thy hand to it.
Behold the prince who undertaketh an enterprise only after consulting with men chosen for their worth:
there is nothing that is impossible for him.
There are enterprises that tempt with a great profit but which perish even the capital itself;
the wise undertake them not.
Behold the men who fear to be ridiculed by others:
they do not take up any enterprise without previous deliberation.
To make war without planning every detail of it before hand is only to transplant thy enemy on carefully prepared soil.
There are things that ought not to be done and if thou do them thou wilt be ruined:
and there are things that ought to be done and if thou do them not thou wilt be ruined also.
Decide not upon any action except after careful deliberation;
he is a fool who undertaketh first and sayeth it in his heart, I shall think afterwards.
Behold the man that goeth not to his work the right way about:
all his labour will be a waste even if numbers come to his aid.
Even in doing good thou mayest err, if thou suit not the benefit to the character of him that receiveth.
Let the thing that thou decidest on be above reproach;
for the world despiseth the man who stoopeth to a thing that is beneath himself.
Weigh justly the difficulty of the enterprise, thy own strength and the strength of thine enemy, and the strength also of your allies:
and then enter thou upon it.
Behold the prince who knoweth his own force and hath learned what he ought to learn, and who over steppeth not the limits of his force and information:
his invasions will never fail.
Many there have been who in the sanguineness of their hearts over-estimated their strength and adventured, but were cut off in the middle.
Behold the men who know not to live in peace, who know not their own measure, and who are full of self conceit;
they will have a swift end.
Put too many of them and even peacocks feathers would break the wagons axle.
Those that have climbed to the top of the tree will lose their lives if they attempt to climb still higher.
Keep thou in thy mind the extent of thy wealth and let thy gifts be commensurate therewith:
that is the way to conserve and divide thy substance.
It mattereth not if the feeder channel is strait, provided that draining channel is not wider.
Behold the man that taketh not account of his measure nor liveth within the bounds thereof;
he may look like prospering, but he will perish leaving no trace behind.
Behold the man that taketh not measure of his wealth and lavishes it on every side with an unsparing hand;
his substance will quickly come to nought.
The crow triumpheth over the owl when it is day;
even so opportunity is a great thing to the prince who would vanquish his enemy.
To follow closely on the pace of Time;
that is the cord that will bind the Goddess of Fortune to thee firmly.
Where is the thing called impossible if thou start on the enterprise with a knowledge of the right season and employ the proper means?
Thou canst conquer even the whole world if thou choose the proper time and the proper objectives.
Those that are intent on conquests will be quitely watching their opportunity:
they will know neither confusion nor hurry.
The ram steppeth back before it delivereth the stunning blow:
even such is the inaction of the man of energy.
The wise show not their anger on the spot:
they will nurse it within hearts and wait for their opportunity.
Bend down before thy adversaries when they are more powerful than thyself:
they can be easily overthrown when thou attackest them at the moment that their power is on the decline.
When thou hast got an unusual chance, hesitate not but straightaway attempt even the impossible.
When the time is against thee feign inaction like the stork:
but when the tide is on, strike with the swiftness of its souse.
Provoke no war and begin no operation except after making a thorough reconnaissance of the theatre of operations.
It is an immense advantage even to the powerful and the strong to be based on fortified places.
Even the weak can hold their own and triumph over a powerful foe if they choose the proper theatre and operate cautiously.
The plans of thy adversaries will be baffled if thou fall back on strong positions already reconnoitred and base thyself on them.
All powerful is the crocodile in deep water:
but out of it, it is plaything of its foes.
The strong-wheeled chariot runneth not on the sea;
for saileth not the ocean going ship, on dry land.
Behold the prince that hath planned everything before hand and striketh at the proper objective:
he wanteth no other ally than his own courage.
If the prince whose army is weak only betaketh himself to a proper theatre of war, all the endeavours even of the strongest foes would be vain against him.
Even if they have no proper defences and other advantages it is hard to beat a people on their own soil.
Behold the high-mettled elephant that hath faced without wincing a whole multitude of lancer:
even a jackal will triumph over him if he is entangled in marshy ground.
Love of the right, gold, pleasure, and fear of life, these four are the tests of a man:
give thy confidence therefore to men that satisfy all these tests.
Behold the man who is born of a good family, who is free from faults and who dreadeth disgrace: he is the man for thee.
Even men of rare learning and of pure hearts will not be found, when thou dost test them, to be absolutely exempt from all ignorance.
Weigh a mans good and weigh his evil:
whichever is more, take that to be his nature.
Dost thou want to find out whether a man is noble or little-minded ? know that conduct is the touchstone of character.
Beware of trusting men that have no kindred:
for their hearts will be without attachment and they will be callous to shame.
If thou choosest a fool for thy confidential adviser because that thou lovest him, he will lead thee to endless follies.
Behold the man that trusteth another without trying him:
he createth endless evils even unto his posterity.
Never trust men without trying them:
and after trying them, give each one of them the work for which he is fit.
To trust a man whom thou hast not tried and to suspect a man whom thou hast found worthy lead alike to endless ills.
Behold the man that seeth the good and seeth the evil also; and chooseth only that which is good:
employ thou him in thy service.
Behold the man that is able to develop the resources of thy kingdom and to cure the ills that may befall it;
set him to manage thy affairs.
Let him alone be selected for service who is well endowed with kindness, and intelligence and decision, and who is free from greed.
Many are the men that satisfy every test and yet alter in the actual performance of duty.
Work should be entrusted to men in consideration of their expert knowledge and capacity for patient exertion, and not of their love towards thy person.
Choose the servant and give him the work for which he is fit:
see that the time is ripe for performance and get him to begin it.
Determine first the capacity of the servant and the work for which he is fit:
and then leave him in responsible charge of the same.
After thou hast decided that a man is fit for an office, raise him to the dignity and give him the conveniences that will enable him to fill that office worthily.
Behold the man who misunderstandeth the liberties taken by the servant who is skilful at his work:
Fortune will depart from him.
Let the prince oversee everything every day for there will be nothing wrong with the country so long as there is nothing wrong with the officers of the state.
Constancy of attachment even in adversity belongeth only unto kindred.
If a man is blessed with kindred whose love for him abateth not, fortunes will never cease to grow.
Behold the man who does not mix freely with his kinsmen and command their affection:
he is like a tank without bonds: the waters of prosperity will flow away from him.
To gather and attach ones kindred to oneself;
that is the use and purpose of prosperity.
If a man have a sweet tongue and a liberal hand his kinsmen will gather round him is serried ranks.
Behold the man that giveth freely without stinting and is never angry:
the world hath none who hath a more attached kindred than he.
The crow concealeth not its food selfishly from its fellows but shareth it lovingly with them:
prosperity will abide only with men of a like nature.
It is good if the prince treateth not all his kinsmen alike. but treateth each differently according to his merit:
for there are many that love to have privileges not shared by others.
The estrangement of a kinsman is easily remedied:
remove the cause of the coolness and he will come back to thee.
When a kinsman that hath broken with thee cometh back to thee for a reason, accept thou him but with caution.
Worse than excessive rage is the unguardedness that cometh of over-weening self-complacency.
A false sense of security killeth glory even as indigence crusheth the understanding.
Glory is not for the unwatchful:
that is the conclusion of every school of thinkers in the world.
Of what avail are fortresses to the cowardly? or abundance of resources to the incautious?
He who faileth to guard against everything beforehand will deplore his negligence when he is surprised by disaster.
If thou relax not in thy vigilance at all times and against all men, there is nothing like it.
Nothing is impossible to the man who can bring unto his work a mind that is ever wakeful and cautious.
The prince should devoteth himself assiduously to works that are commended by the wise:
if he neglect them he will not escape suffering in any of his seven reincarnations.
When thou art tempted to be self-complacent and elated, call to thy mind those that have perished by their supineness and negligence.
Verily it is easy for a man to achieve all that he desireth, provided he keepeth his purpose constantly before his mind.
Deliberate well and lean not to either side:
be impartial and consult with men of law: that is the way to administer justice.
The world looketh up to the rain cloud for life:
even so do men look up to the sceptre of the prince for protection.
The sceptre of the prince is the mainstay of the science of the Brahmans and of righteousness also.
Behold the noble prince who ruleth the people of his dominions with loving care:
sovereignty will never depart from him.
Behold the prince who wieldeth the sceptre in accordance with the law:
seasonal rains and rich harvests have their home in his land.
It is not the lance that bringeth victory unto the prince:
it is rather his sceptre, and that provided it is straight and leaneth not to either side.
The prince is the protector of all his people:
and him his sceptre will guard, provided he alloweth it not ever to lean to either side.
Behold the prince who is not easy of access and who judgeth not causes with care:
he will fall from his place and perish even when he hath no enemy.
Behold the prince that guardeth his subjects from enemies both within and without:
if he punish them when they go wrong it is not a blemish: it is his duty.
Punishing the wicked with death is like the removing of weeds from the cornfield.
Behold the prince who oppresseth his subjects and doth iniquity;
he is worse than an assassin.
A request from him who holdeth the sceptre is like the stand and deliver of the highway robber.
Behold the prince who doth not oversee his administration every day and remove the irregularities therein:
his sovereignty will wear away day by day.
Behold the thoughtless prince whose rule swerveth from the ways of justice:
he will lose his kingdom and his substance also.
Verily it is the tears of those groaning under oppression that wear away the prosperity of the prince.
It is just rule that bringeth renown unto princes:
but an unjust government darkeneth their glory.
How fareth the earth under a rainless sky? even so fare the people under the rule of a cruel prince.
The condition of the rich man is more galling than that of the poor under the rule of a cruel prince.
The heavens will not send showers in their season if the prince swerveth from justice and right.
The udders of the cow will be dried up and the Brahman will forget his science if the Prince ruleth not with justice.
The prince shall measure the guilt of the offender and punish him so that he offend not again:
but the punishment shall not be excessive.
Those that desire that their power should last, let them brandish the rod smartly but lay it on soft.
Behold the prince who ruleth with a rod of iron and causeth terror to his people:
he will stand without a friend and perish forthwith.
Behold the prince whose cruelty is a byword among his people:
he will lose his kingdom betimes and his days will be shortened also.
Behold the dour-faced prince who is inaccessible to his people:
the wealth in his hands is like treasure guarded by a demon.
If the prince is harsh of word and unforgiving, his prosperity, be it ever so great, will come to an end quickly.
Words that are harsh and punishments that are excessive are the files that file away the iron of power.
Behold the prince who will not take counsel with his ministers but who falleth into a passion when his projects fail:
his prosperity will wane away.
Behold the prince who looketh not to his defences while yet there is time:
when he is surprised by a war he will be seized with trembling and perish quickly.
Tyranny that allieth itself to fools and charlatans is the only burden under which the earth groaneth:
there is none other besides.
Behold that ravishing Beauty called considerateness:
if the world runneth on smoothly it is all owing to her.
In considerateness have the amenities of life their existence:
those who possess it not are a burden unto the earth.
What is the worth of the song that cannot be sung? and what is the worth of the eye that showeth not indulgence?
What is the use of eyes that merely show in the face, if they show not consideration for others according to their measure?
Considerateness is the ornament of the eye:
the eye that hath it not will be looked upon as a mere sore.
Behold the men who have eyes, but which show not consideration towards others:
verily they are no better than trees fixed in the earth.
Verily they are blind, those who show not consideration towards others:
and there are none that truly see but are indulgent to others faults.
Behold the man who can be considerate towards others without derogating from any of his duties:
he will inherit the earth.
It is nobility to forbear and show indulgence even unto those that have offended thee.
Those who desire to be styled the very pink of courtesy will drink off even the poison that hath been mixed for them before their own eyes.
Let the prince understand that political science and his Intelligence corps are the eyes wherewith he seeth.
It is the duty of the prince to learn betimes everything that befalleth every man and every day.
Behold the prince that learneth not the happenings about him by means of scouts and spies:
conquests are not for him.
The prince shall set spies to watch closely the officers of the realm, his own kindred, and his enemies.
Behold the man who can wear an unsuspicious appearance, who will not know confusion before any man, and who can guard his secrets from ever leaking out:
he is the proper man for the work of Intelligence.
Spies and scouts should disguise themselves as ascetics and holy men, and their investigation should be thorough;
and whatever is done them they should not let out their secrets.
Behold the man who can draw out secrets from others and whose information is ever unconfused and clear:
he is the man for the work of intelligence.
Even the information that hath been obtained by a spy should be tested by that of another.
See that no spy knoweth the others engaged in the same work:
when three reports agree thou mayest give credence to them.
Reward not openly thy officers of Intelligence;
for if thou do, thou merely lettest out thy own secret.
Those that possess energy are alone to be called rich:
as to those that possess it not, do they really possess what they own?
Energy alone can be called a mans wealth:
for riches endure not for ever and will depart from him one day.
Behold the men that hold in their hands the resource called unremitting energy:
they will never despair, saying Alas, we are ruined.
Behold the man who remitteth not ever from exertion:
Good Fortune inquireth the way to his home and entereth there.
The water with which a plant is watered is the measure of the luxuriance of its flower:
Even so, the spirit of a man is the measure of his fortunes.
Let all thy purposes be grand:
for then, even if they fail, thy glory will tarnish never.
Men of spirit lose not their heart when they meet with defeat:
the elephant planteth his legs only more firmly when he is hit by the deep - piercing arrow.
Behold the men that are wanting in energy:
the glory of an exhaustless liberality can never be theirs.
What availeth his size and his sharp tapering tusks? The heart of the elephant sinketh when he seeth the tiger preparing to spring.
Exuberance of spirit, that alone is strength:
those that have it not are mere stocks: their human bodies alone make the difference.
The perennial light called Dynasty will be extinguished if it is invaded by the foul vapour of sloth.
Let them call sloth by its real name and avoid it, those who desire to establish their family on a solid foundation.
Behold the fool who huggeth assassin sloth unto his heart:
his dynasty will fall even before his day is ended.
Behold the men who are sunk in sloth and who turn not their hand to high and noble undertakings:
their house will go to ruin and their vices will grow apace.
Procrastination, forgetfulness, sloth and sleep, those four are the cosy pleasure boats of those that are fated to perish.
The slothful can never thrive in the world even though they have the favour of princes.
Behold the men who are slothful and who turn not their hand to great undertakings:
they will have to listen to much reproof and contumely.
If sloth find a home in a family, the family will soon be in bondage to its foes.
The afflictions that may have befallen a mans family will cease to exist the moment he giveth up sloth.
Behold the prince that knoweth not sloth:
he will bring within his sway all that hath been measured by the steps of Trivikrama.
Shrink not from any work saying, it is impossible:
for labour will give thee the strength to achieve everything.
Beware of leaving any work unfinished:
for the world careth not for those that do not complete the work that they have once begun.
The proud pleasure of being able to serve all men belongeth only to the greatness that shrinketh not from any exertion.
Like unto a sword in the hands of the eunuch is the liberality of the indolent man: it will not endure.
The man who loveth not pleasure but loveth work is a pillar of strength unto his friends and will wipe away their tears of grief.
Industry is the mother of Prosperity:
but Indolence only bringeth forth Penury and Destitution.
In sloth hath the Genius of wretchedness her home:
but the Lotus born One resideth in the labour of his who yieldeth not to sloth.
It is no shame if fortune faileth a man:
but it is a disgrace if he abstain deliberately from exertion.
Even though the Gods be against, Industry is bound to pay the wages of labour.
They will snap their fingers even at Destiny who succumb not to it but labour unremittingly in despite of it.
When thou meetest with misfortune face it with thy best smile:
for there is nothing like a smile to enable a man to hold his own against it.
A whole sea of troubles will abase themselves the moment a shifty mind collecteth itself to face them.
Troubles they send away troubled who trouble not themselves at the sight of troubles.
Behold the man who is prepared to strain his every nerve like bull buffalo to wade through every difficulty:
he may meet with obstacles but he will send them away disappointed.
Behold the man whose heart sinketh not even at a whole host of troubles arrayed against him:
the obstacles in his path have themselves met with an obstacle.
The men that exult not at good fortune, can they ever have to fret themselves saying, Alas! we are ruined?
The wise know that the body is a target unto misfortune:
and so they worry themselves not when they meet with a calamity.
Behold the man who loveth not pleasure and who knoweth that difficulties are a part of the law of things:
he smarteth not ever under any check.
The man who runneth not after pleasure in the day of success suffereth not pain in the day of failure.
Behold the man who looketh upon the stress and strain of exertion as a veritable joy:
he will be extolled by his very enemies.
Behold the man who can judge aright the (men and) means of achieving great enterprises, the proper season to commence them and (the worth of) the enterprises themselves:
he is the proper man for thy council.

Study, resolution, manly exertion and loving attention to the welfare of the people, these, along with the five make the qualifications of the councillor. (viz. men, means, season, plan and the enterprises themselves see ).
poruttalum vallatu amaiccu. He is the able minister who possesseth the capacity to disunite allies, to cherish and keep up existing friendships, and to reunite those who have become enemies.
collalum vallatu amaiccu. Judgement in the choice of projects and the means of their execution, and positiveness in the expression of opinion are necessary qualities in the councillor.
Behold the man who knoweth the law and aboundeth in instruction, is deliberate in his speech and always understandeth what is fit for each occasion:
he is the counillor for thee.
What is there that is too subtle for men who add knowledge of books unto natural intelligence?
Even though thou art wise in thy knowledge of books, gather thou the wisdom of experience and act in accordance therewith.
The prince may be a fool and may thwart him at every step:
but the duty of the councillor is always to point to him what is just and proper.
Behold the minister that sitteth in the council and plotteth the ruin of his prince:
he is more dangerous than seven hundred million enemies.
The irresolute may even plan perfectly:
but they will waver in the course of the execution and will never accomplish their designs.
The blessing of the tongue is a blessing indeed:
for it is a blessing apart and formeth not part of other blessings.
Prosperity and ruin are in the power of the tongue:
guard thou therefore against imprudence of speech.
Behold the speech that bindeth friends more closely and softeneth the hearts of even enemies:
that alone is worthy of the name.
Weigh each circumstance aright and then speak the speech that is fit:
for the increase of righteousness and profit there is no other thing of more worth to thee than it.
Speak thou the speech that cannot be silenced by any other speech.
To speak so as to bind to ones self ones hearers and to take the substance in the words of others, that is the part of the consummate statesman.
Behold the man who is eloquent of speech and knoweth neither confusion nor fear:
it is impossible for anyone to beat him in debate.
Behold the men whose speech is well-ordered and couched in persuasive language:
the world will be at their beck and call.
Verily they have a passion for much speaking who know not to say their mind in few and well-chosen words.
Behold the men who cannot expound unto others the knowledge that they have acquired:
they are like unto the flower that hath blossomed on its bunch but giveth forth no fragrance.
Alliances bring success unto a man:
but purity of action fulfilleth his every desire.
Always turn thy face away from those deeds that bring not forth lasting good as well as glory.
Those that desire to rise in the world, let them abjure all action that can tarnish their glory.
Behold the men who see things in their right proportions:
even when fallen on evil days stoop not to action that is dishonourable and mean.
Let not a man do those things which make him cry afterwards, what is it that I have done? and if he hath done any such thing, it will be good for him if he doth it not once again.
Let not a man do those things that good men condemn, even to save the mother that bore him, from starvation.
The indigence of the worthy is better far than wealth that is amassed by dishonourable means.
Behold the men that shun not those things that are forbidden by good morals:
they will come to grief even if they succeed in their designs.
All that is wrung in the midst of tears will depart also accompanied by weepings:
but that which is acquired by righteous ways, even if lost in the middle, increaseth in the latter end.
To try to lay by wealth by means of guile is like trying to preserve water in a pot of clay that is not baked.
Greatness of achievement is nought else but the greatness of the will that striveth therefor:
all other things come not near the mark.
To avoid all action that is bound to fail and not to turn away from ones purpose because of obstacles:
these two are said to be the guiding principles of the wise.
The man of action letteth his purpose appear only when that purpose is achieved:
for an untimely disclosure may create obstacles that cannot be surmounted.
To say a thing is easy for any man:
but to do it in the manner undertaken is a rare thing indeed.
Behold the man who hath acquired a name for the doing of great deeds:
his services will be greatly in request with the prince and will be esteemed by all.
That which they will, men acquire even in the manner that they will, provided they will with all their might.
Despise not a man for his look:
for there are men who are even as the axle - pin of the mighty rolling car.
When thou hast resolved upon a thing with all thy wits about thee, waver not but pursue thy purpose with vigour.
Take up the doing of works that increase happiness:
and even if thou have to suffer cruel mortification in the doing of them, steel thy heart and persevere to the end.
Behold the men that lack decision of character:
whatever greatness they may have achieved in other directions the world will not care for them.
The end of all deliberation is to arrive at a decision:
and when a decision is come to, it is wrong to delay the execution thereof.
Do with deliberation those things that ought to be done in a leisurely way:
but put not off even for a moment those things that require prompt action.
Go straight for the goal whenever circumstances permit:
but when circumstances are against, follow along the path that offereth the least resistance.
Unfinished work and enemies that are left unsubdued are like unextinguished sparks of fire:
